questions.explanation: In which is the formal equivalent of 'where' for a thing or place.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly uses 'on which'?
options: The day on which we met changed my life.
The day on that we met changed my life.
The day on where we met changed my life.
The day on whom we met changed my life.
questions.explanation: On which is the formal structure for a time relationship involving a day.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly uses 'for which'?
options: The reason for which he resigned was never explained.
The reason for that he resigned was never explained.
The reason for where he resigned was never explained.
The reason for whom he resigned was never explained.
questions.explanation: For which is a formal alternative to 'why' after 'reason'.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly uses 'what' rather than 'which'?
options: The information what I need is missing.
The information what I need it is missing.
What the information I need is missing.
questions.explanation: What introduces a free relative clause without a separate antecedent.

questions.questionText: Which sentence incorrectly uses a relative pronoun because an antecedent is already present?
options: Whatever he says will be recorded.
The statement which he made was surprising.
The statement what he made was surprising.
questions.explanation: The antecedent 'statement' is already present, so which or that should be used instead of what.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly uses 'whoever'?
options: Whoever finishes the task first will receive the prize.
Whoever the task first will receive the prize.
Whoever which finishes the task will receive the prize.
Whoever whose finishes the task will receive the prize.
questions.explanation: Whoever means 'any person who' and functions as the subject.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly uses 'whatever'?
options: Whatever you decide will be acceptable.
Whatever who you decide will be acceptable.
Whatever which you decide will be acceptable.
Whatever whose you decide will be acceptable.
questions.explanation: Whatever means 'anything that' or 'no matter what'.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly uses 'whichever'?
options: Whichever of these two routes you choose will work.
Whoever of these two routes you choose will work.
Whatever of these two routes you choose will work.
Whose of these two routes you choose will work.
questions.explanation: Whichever refers to one choice from a limited set.

questions.questionText: Which sentence contains a subject-verb agreement error inside the relative clause?
options: The engineer who designs the system is experienced.
The engineers who design the system are experienced.
The engineer who design the system is experienced.
The engineers who design the system work efficiently.
questions.explanation: The singular antecedent 'engineer' requires 'designs'.

questions.questionText: Which sentence is grammatically correct?
options: The group of students who studies together is successful.
The group of students who study together is successful.
The group of students who studies together are successful.
The group of students which study together are successful.
questions.explanation: Here 'who' refers to the plural 'students', so 'study' is correct; the main subject 'group' takes 'is'.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly uses a defining relative clause with no commas?
options: The employees who completed the training received certificates.
The employees, who completed the training, received certificates.
The employees who completed the training, received certificates.
The employees, who completed the training received certificates.
questions.explanation: The relative clause identifies which employees, so it is defining and requires no commas.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly uses a non-defining relative clause?
options: Ethiopia which has a long history attracts many researchers.
Ethiopia, which has a long history, attracts many researchers.
Ethiopia that has a long history attracts many researchers.
Ethiopia, that has a long history, attracts many researchers.
questions.explanation: The proper noun already identifies the country, so the additional information is non-defining.

questions.questionText: Which sentence is grammatically incorrect because the relative pronoun is omitted as the subject?
options: The book I bought was expensive.
The person I met was friendly.
The man lives next door is a doctor.
The movie we watched was excellent.
questions.explanation: The omitted relative pronoun would be the subject of 'lives', so it cannot normally be omitted.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly omits the relative pronoun?
options: The scientist discovered the formula won an award.
The scientist I interviewed won an award.
The scientist works here won an award.
The scientist invented the formula won an award.
questions.explanation: In 'the scientist I interviewed', the omitted relative pronoun is the object of 'interviewed'.

questions.questionText: Which sentence contains a correct formal relative structure?
options: The researcher with whom I collaborated published a paper.
The researcher with that I collaborated published a paper.
The researcher whom with I collaborated published a paper.
The researcher with who I collaborated published a paper.
questions.explanation: With whom is the formal structure for a person after the preposition 'with'.

questions.questionText: Which sentence contains an incorrect relative pronoun?
options: The professor whose lecture I attended was excellent.
The professor whom I contacted replied quickly.
The professor which teaches physics is absent.
The professor who teaches physics is absent.
questions.explanation: Which is normally used for things and animals, not people.

questions.questionText: Which sentence contains an incorrect use of 'whom'?
options: The person whom I invited arrived early.
The person to whom I spoke was helpful.
The person whom called me was helpful.
The person whom we interviewed was qualified.
questions.explanation: Whom is an object, but here the relative word is the subject of 'called', so who is required.

questions.questionText: Which sentence contains an incorrect use of 'whose'?
options: The student whose laptop broke reported the problem.
The company whose offices are nearby hired new workers.
The teacher whose helped me was kind.
The woman whose son is a doctor lives here.
questions.explanation: Whose must be followed by a possessed noun, not directly by the verb 'helped'.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly uses 'whose' with a non-human antecedent?
options: The company whose headquarters are in Addis Ababa expanded rapidly.
The company whose is in Addis Ababa expanded rapidly.
The company whose it operates in Addis Ababa expanded rapidly.
The company whom headquarters are in Addis Ababa expanded rapidly.
questions.explanation: Whose can express possession or association with things and organizations.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly uses a reduced passive relative clause?
options: The documents submitted yesterday are being reviewed.
The documents submitting yesterday are being reviewed.
The documents submit yesterday are being reviewed.
The documents which submitting yesterday are being reviewed.
questions.explanation: 'Which were submitted' can be reduced to 'submitted'.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly uses a reduced active relative clause?
options: The students studying in the library are preparing for exams.
The students studied in the library are preparing for exams.
The students study in the library are preparing for exams.
The students whom studying in the library are preparing for exams.
questions.explanation: 'Students who are studying' can be reduced to 'students studying'.

questions.questionText: Which sentence has the correct relative-clause structure?
options: The woman who I believe is the manager arrived.
The woman whom I believe is the manager arrived.
The woman which I believe is the manager arrived.
The woman whose I believe is the manager arrived.
questions.explanation: Who is the subject of 'is the manager'; 'I believe' is inserted before the predicate.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly uses 'which' to refer to a thing in a non-defining clause?
options: The laptop, which I bought last year, still works perfectly.
The laptop, that I bought last year, still works perfectly.
The laptop which, I bought last year still works perfectly.
The laptop, who I bought last year, still works perfectly.
questions.explanation: Which is appropriate for a non-defining clause referring to a thing.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly uses an omitted object relative pronoun?
options: The article I read yesterday was controversial.
The article I wrote yesterday was controversial.
The article I published yesterday was controversial.
questions.explanation: In each sentence, the article is the object of the verb, so the relative pronoun can be omitted.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly uses 'where' and not 'when'?
options: This is the laboratory where the experiment was conducted.
This is the laboratory when the experiment was conducted.
This is the laboratory whose the experiment was conducted.
This is the laboratory whom the experiment was conducted.
questions.explanation: Where refers to the location of the experiment.

title: Ethiopian English University Entrance Practice Test 4 2024
description: Ethiopian English University Entrance Practice Test 4 2024 featuring 100 authentic questions with step-by-step solutions. Designed for Ethiopian national exam mastery.

questions.questionText: The laboratory lights are on, and the technician's car is outside. She _____ be inside.
questions.explanation: The evidence strongly supports the conclusion, so must expresses strong present deduction.

questions.questionText: Nobody has seen Daniel today, but his phone is connected to the office Wi-Fi. He _____ be working there.
questions.explanation: The evidence suggests a possibility but does not prove it, so might is appropriate.

questions.questionText: The office is completely locked, and the security guard confirmed that everyone left. They _____ be inside.
questions.explanation: The evidence makes their being inside impossible or extremely unlikely, so can't expresses negative deduction.

questions.questionText: The weather forecast is uncertain, so it _____ rain this afternoon.
questions.explanation: Might expresses an uncertain possibility.

questions.questionText: The examination begins at eight, so the students _____ be in the examination hall by now.
questions.explanation: Should expresses an expected or probable present situation.

questions.questionText: The door is open, but nobody is answering. They _____ be sleeping.
questions.explanation: May expresses a possible explanation for the situation.

questions.questionText: The road is completely flooded. The bridge _____ be safe to cross.
questions.explanation: The evidence strongly suggests that the bridge is not safe, so can't expresses negative deduction.

questions.questionText: She has not answered any messages all morning. She _____ be busy.
questions.explanation: The evidence gives a possible explanation, but not a certain conclusion.

questions.questionText: The ground is wet even though nobody watered the garden. It _____ have rained.
questions.explanation: The wet ground is strong evidence that rain occurred, so must have rained expresses past deduction.

questions.questionText: James arrived two hours late. He _____ have missed the earlier bus.
questions.explanation: Missing the earlier bus is one possible explanation, so may have missed is appropriate.

questions.questionText: The lights were switched off when I arrived, but the door was unlocked. The owner _____ have left recently.
questions.explanation: The evidence allows this as a possible past explanation, so might have left works.

questions.questionText: Sara was with me throughout the entire evening. She _____ have committed the crime at 9 p.m.
questions.explanation: Being with the speaker provides strong evidence that the past event was impossible, so couldn't have committed is correct.

questions.questionText: He looks exhausted after working a twelve-hour shift. He _____ be tired.
questions.explanation: The evidence strongly supports the conclusion that he is tired.

questions.questionText: The manager's office is empty, but her computer is still running. She _____ have gone out briefly.
questions.explanation: Going out briefly is a possible explanation, so might have gone is suitable.

questions.questionText: The train has already departed, so the passengers _____ have missed it.
questions.explanation: May have missed expresses a possible past event.

questions.questionText: The entire street is covered in snow. It _____ have snowed heavily during the night.
questions.explanation: The evidence strongly supports the conclusion that heavy snow occurred.

questions.questionText: He is currently in Nairobi, so he _____ be attending the meeting in Addis Ababa at this moment.
questions.explanation: His location provides strong evidence that he cannot be at the meeting.

questions.questionText: The baby is unusually quiet. She _____ be sleeping.
questions.explanation: Sleeping is a possible explanation, so might be sleeping is appropriate.

questions.questionText: The computer is still warm and the document is open. Someone _____ have been using it recently.
questions.explanation: The evidence strongly indicates recent use, so must have been using expresses strong deduction.

questions.questionText: The children are not in the classroom, but their bags are on the desks. They _____ be outside.
questions.explanation: Being outside is one possible explanation, so might be outside is correct.

questions.questionText: The package was sent five days ago. It _____ arrive tomorrow.
questions.explanation: Should expresses an expected or probable future result.

questions.questionText: The professor has not arrived yet, but the lecture starts in five minutes. He _____ arrive soon.
questions.explanation: Should expresses expectation or probability.

questions.questionText: The students have been studying since early morning. They _____ be exhausted by now.
questions.explanation: The evidence strongly supports the conclusion that they are exhausted.

questions.questionText: The lights in the house are off, but someone may still be inside. They _____ be asleep.
questions.explanation: Might expresses a tentative possibility.

questions.questionText: There is no sign of John at the station. He _____ have taken a different train.
questions.explanation: Taking a different train is one possible explanation.

questions.questionText: She knew the meeting had been cancelled, so she _____ have gone to the office for it.
questions.explanation: The evidence makes it impossible or extremely unlikely that she went there for the meeting.

questions.questionText: The roads are unusually quiet tonight. There _____ be fewer people travelling because of the storm.
questions.explanation: Fewer travellers is a possible explanation, so might is suitable.

questions.questionText: The electricity has been off for six hours. The refrigerator _____ still be working normally.
questions.explanation: The lack of electricity makes normal operation impossible or extremely unlikely.

questions.questionText: The students have already submitted their papers. They _____ have finished the examination.
questions.explanation: Submission of the papers provides strong evidence that they finished.

questions.questionText: The weather radar shows a large storm approaching. It _____ rain heavily tonight.
questions.explanation: Heavy rain is a possible future situation, so could expresses possibility.

questions.questionText: The museum normally closes at six, so it _____ be open at eight unless there is a special event.
questions.explanation: Under the stated normal circumstances, being open at eight is strongly ruled out.

questions.questionText: I cannot find my keys anywhere. I _____ have left them at the restaurant.
questions.explanation: Leaving them at the restaurant is a possible past explanation.

questions.questionText: Her suitcase is missing from the room. She _____ have taken it with her.
questions.explanation: Taking the suitcase is a possible explanation, so may have taken is appropriate.

questions.questionText: The witness saw the suspect in another city at the exact time of the robbery. He _____ have committed the robbery then.
questions.explanation: The evidence makes the past event impossible or extremely unlikely.

questions.questionText: The children are making no noise, and their bedroom door is closed. They _____ be sleeping.
questions.explanation: The evidence strongly supports the deduction that they are sleeping.

questions.questionText: The roads are wet, but the weather report says it has not rained in the area. Someone _____ have washed the roads.
questions.explanation: Washing the roads is a possible explanation, so might have washed is appropriate.

questions.questionText: The office lights are off and the doors are locked. The employees _____ have gone home.
questions.explanation: The evidence strongly supports the conclusion that they went home.

questions.questionText: The manager has not replied to the message. She _____ be in a meeting.
questions.explanation: Being in a meeting is a possible explanation.

questions.questionText: The entire team has disappeared from the building. They _____ be attending the emergency meeting.
questions.explanation: The evidence strongly supports this present deduction.

questions.questionText: The plane left at noon, and the airport records show that she checked in. She _____ have boarded the plane.
questions.explanation: The available evidence strongly supports the conclusion that she boarded.

questions.questionText: Nobody knows where Ahmed is. He _____ have gone to the library.
questions.explanation: Going to the library is one possible explanation.

questions.questionText: The lights in the laboratory are on, but the laboratory is normally closed at night. A researcher _____ be working late.
questions.explanation: Working late is a possible explanation for the lights being on.

questions.questionText: The car is still in the garage, so its owner _____ have driven it to work this morning.
questions.explanation: The car remaining in the garage strongly contradicts the idea that the owner drove it.

questions.questionText: The students look confused because the instructions were unclear. They _____ have misunderstood the question.
questions.explanation: Misunderstanding the question is a possible explanation.

questions.questionText: The package has not arrived after three weeks. It _____ have been lost in the mail.
questions.explanation: Being lost is a possible explanation for the delay.

questions.questionText: The lights are on, the door is open, and music is playing. Someone _____ be inside.
questions.explanation: Several pieces of evidence strongly support the conclusion that someone is inside.

questions.questionText: The security camera shows that the gate was never opened. The suspect _____ have entered through that gate.
questions.explanation: The evidence makes entering through that gate impossible or extremely unlikely.

questions.questionText: The clouds are extremely dark, and a storm warning has been issued. It _____ rain soon.
questions.explanation: Rain is a strong possibility, so could is appropriate.

questions.questionText: The road is blocked by a fallen tree. The bus _____ arrive on time.
questions.explanation: The obstruction makes arriving on time impossible or extremely unlikely.

questions.questionText: The doctor has examined the patient and found a high fever. The patient _____ be suffering from an infection.
questions.explanation: An infection is a possible explanation, so might be is appropriate.

questions.questionText: The student's desk is covered with books and notes. He _____ be preparing for the examination.
questions.explanation: The evidence strongly supports the deduction that he is preparing.

questions.questionText: The bus was delayed by an accident. We _____ arrive later than expected.
questions.explanation: Arriving later is a possible consequence of the accident.

questions.questionText: The shop has been closed all day. The owner _____ be away.
questions.explanation: The owner's absence is a possible explanation.

questions.questionText: The report contains several pages of calculations. The researcher _____ have spent many hours preparing it.
questions.explanation: The report provides strong evidence for the deduction that considerable time was spent preparing it.

questions.questionText: The phone has been switched off since yesterday. She _____ be avoiding calls.
questions.explanation: Avoiding calls is one possible explanation.

questions.questionText: The classroom windows are open and the curtains are moving. Someone _____ have opened them.
questions.explanation: The evidence strongly suggests that someone opened the windows.

questions.questionText: The road signs indicate that the highway is closed. We _____ use that route tonight.
questions.explanation: The closure strongly indicates that using the route is impossible or not possible under the circumstances.

questions.questionText: The child has been awake since dawn. He _____ be tired now.
questions.explanation: The evidence strongly supports the conclusion that he is tired.

questions.questionText: The meeting ended at four, but Sarah has not returned yet. She _____ have gone somewhere else afterward.
questions.explanation: Going somewhere else is a possible explanation.

questions.questionText: The lights in the stadium are off and the gates are locked. The match _____ be taking place now.
questions.explanation: The evidence strongly indicates that the match is not taking place.

questions.questionText: The professor's car is outside his house, but nobody has seen him. He _____ be at home.
questions.explanation: Being at home is possible, but the evidence does not establish it with certainty.

questions.questionText: The student received a very high mark after studying all weekend. She _____ have prepared thoroughly.
questions.explanation: The result and previous information strongly support this past deduction.

questions.questionText: The witness was abroad during the entire month. He _____ have seen the incident in person.
questions.explanation: Being abroad during the entire period makes personally seeing the incident impossible or extremely unlikely.

questions.questionText: The package tracking system says 'out for delivery.' The package _____ arrive today.
questions.explanation: Should expresses an expected or probable result.

questions.questionText: The weather is changing rapidly. The flight _____ be delayed.
questions.explanation: A delay is a possible future event.

questions.questionText: The laboratory was locked from the outside all night. Nobody _____ have entered through the main door.
questions.explanation: The locked door provides strong evidence that entering through it was impossible.

questions.questionText: The children have left their shoes by the swimming pool. They _____ be swimming now.
questions.explanation: The shoes provide strong evidence supporting the deduction that they are swimming.

questions.questionText: The teacher is not in the classroom, and her car is missing. She _____ have gone home.
questions.explanation: Going home is a possible past explanation.

questions.questionText: The workers have been drilling since morning. They _____ be exhausted.
questions.explanation: The evidence strongly supports the conclusion that they are exhausted.

questions.questionText: The computer screen is still active, but the employee is not at the desk. He _____ be taking a break.
questions.explanation: Taking a break is one possible explanation.

questions.questionText: The streets were completely dry at midnight, but they are flooded now. It _____ have rained heavily overnight.
questions.explanation: The change from dry to flooded strongly supports the deduction that heavy rain occurred.

questions.questionText: The suspect was recorded entering the building at 8:00, while the crime occurred at 9:00. He _____ have been inside the building at 9:00.
questions.explanation: The available evidence does not allow the conclusion that he was outside; however, if the context states he left before 9, can't would be needed. Here the sentence does not establish that, so this option is not sufficiently supported.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly expresses a strong deduction about the present?
questions.explanation: A modal is followed by the base form, and be is required before an adjective.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly expresses a possible past event?
questions.explanation: The correct perfect modal structure is might + have + V3.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly expresses a strong deduction about a past event?
options: They must to have gone home.
questions.explanation: Past deduction uses must + have + past participle.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly expresses a negative deduction about the present?
options: She can't to be at home.
questions.explanation: Can't be is the standard structure for strong negative present deduction.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly expresses a possible ongoing action?
questions.explanation: Present continuous possibility uses modal + be + V-ing.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly expresses a strong deduction about an ongoing past action?
questions.explanation: Past continuous deduction uses must + have been + V-ing.

questions.questionText: Which sentence expresses general possibility rather than a specific uncertain event?
options: She can be at home tonight.
questions.explanation: Can commonly expresses general or theoretical possibility.

questions.questionText: Which sentence best expresses a specific uncertain future possibility?
questions.explanation: May is a standard modal for specific uncertain future possibility.

questions.questionText: Which sentence expresses expectation rather than a very strong deduction?
options: She must be home by now.
She should be home by now.
She can't be home by now.
She couldn't be home by now.
questions.explanation: Should expresses an expected or probable situation and is weaker than must.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly distinguishes deduction from obligation?
options: You must be tired after the journey.
You must to be tired after the journey.
You must being tired after the journey.
You must have to be tired after the journey.
questions.explanation: Must be can express a strong logical deduction based on evidence.

questions.questionText: Which sentence expresses prohibition rather than negative deduction?
questions.explanation: Mustn't expresses prohibition, whereas can't is used for negative deduction.

questions.questionText: Which sentence expresses a possible past explanation?
options: He must have missed the bus.
He might have missed the bus.
He can't have missed the bus.
He should have missed the bus.
questions.explanation: Might have missed expresses uncertainty about what happened.

questions.questionText: Which sentence expresses an unrealized past possibility?
options: He could have won the race, but he fell.
He could be winning the race now.
questions.explanation: The sentence states that winning was possible but did not happen.

questions.questionText: Which sentence most clearly expresses a possible explanation?
options: The lights are off. They could be asleep.
The lights are off. They must be asleep.
The lights are off. They can't be asleep.
The lights are off. They should be asleep.
questions.explanation: Could presents being asleep as one possible explanation.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly expresses a negative deduction about a past event?
questions.explanation: Negative past deduction uses can't + have + V3.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly expresses past ongoing possibility?
questions.explanation: Past continuous possibility uses may + have been + V-ing.

questions.questionText: The lights have been on all night, but nobody answers the door. The residents _____ have been sleeping.
questions.explanation: Sleeping is a possible explanation, so might have been sleeping is appropriate.

questions.questionText: The workers' tools are still on the site, and their cars are parked outside. They _____ have left for the day.
questions.explanation: The evidence makes it possible that they have not left, so might not have left is appropriate.

questions.questionText: The alarm is ringing, but nobody is answering the phone. The security guard _____ be investigating it.
questions.explanation: Investigating the alarm is one possible explanation.

questions.questionText: The student submitted an empty answer sheet. He _____ have understood the questions.
questions.explanation: The evidence strongly suggests that he did not understand the questions.

questions.questionText: The car's engine is still warm even though the driver is absent. He _____ have driven it recently.
questions.explanation: The warm engine provides strong evidence of recent driving.

questions.questionText: The student is not answering because his phone is switched off. He _____ be studying without interruptions.
questions.explanation: Studying without interruptions is a possible explanation.

questions.questionText: The teacher has already marked all the papers. She _____ have worked for several hours.
questions.explanation: The completed work strongly supports the deduction that she worked for several hours.

questions.questionText: The restaurant is full and people are waiting outside. The food _____ be popular.
questions.explanation: The evidence strongly supports the conclusion that the food is popular.

questions.questionText: The student's computer has crashed, so he _____ have lost some of his work.
questions.explanation: Losing some work is a possible consequence of the crash.

questions.questionText: The road is empty even though it is normally busy at this hour. There _____ be an accident ahead.
questions.explanation: An accident is a possible explanation for the unusual traffic conditions.

questions.questionText: The house has been dark and locked for several days. The owners _____ be away.
questions.explanation: Being away is a possible explanation, but the evidence does not prove it.

questions.questionText: The examination hall is empty and all the answer sheets have been collected. The examination _____ have ended.
questions.explanation: The evidence strongly supports the conclusion that the examination has ended.

title: Ethiopian English University Entrance Practice Test 5 2024
description: Ethiopian English University Entrance Practice Test 5 2024 featuring 100 authentic questions with step-by-step solutions. Designed for Ethiopian national exam mastery.

questions.questionText: Both the principal and the teachers ___ responsible for the decision.
questions.explanation: Both...and joins two subjects, so a plural verb is required.

questions.questionText: Either the students or the teacher ___ responsible for collecting the papers.
questions.explanation: With either...or, the verb commonly agrees with the nearer subject, teacher.

questions.questionText: Neither the manager nor the workers ___ available yesterday.
questions.explanation: The nearer subject, workers, is plural, so were is used.

questions.questionText: She is interested in both learning languages ___ studying history.
questions.explanation: The fixed pair is both...and.

questions.questionText: You can ___ submit the assignment online or hand it to the instructor.
questions.explanation: Either...or presents two alternatives.

questions.questionText: He speaks ___ Arabic nor Italian fluently.
questions.explanation: Neither is paired with nor to express two negative alternatives.

questions.questionText: The new policy is not only controversial ___ also difficult to implement.
questions.explanation: The fixed emphatic pair is not only...but also.

questions.questionText: I cannot decide ___ to accept the offer or reject it.
questions.explanation: Whether...or introduces alternatives being considered.

questions.questionText: I would rather remain at home ___ go out in the storm.
questions.explanation: Would rather is followed by than when expressing preference.

questions.questionText: No sooner had the lecture started ___ the electricity failed.
questions.explanation: No sooner is paired with than.

questions.questionText: Hardly had we reached the station ___ the train departed.
questions.explanation: Hardly is normally paired with when.

questions.questionText: Scarcely had she opened the door ___ the alarm sounded.
questions.explanation: Scarcely is paired with when.

questions.questionText: Which sentence has correct parallel structure?
options: She enjoys both reading and to write.
She enjoys both reading and writing.
She enjoys both to read and writing.
She enjoys both read and writing.
questions.explanation: Reading and writing are both gerunds, creating parallel structure.

questions.questionText: Which sentence is grammatically correct?
options: Both the nurse and the doctor is present.
Both the nurse and the doctor are present.
Both the nurse or the doctor are present.
Both the nurse nor the doctor is present.
questions.explanation: Both...and requires a plural verb when joining two subjects.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly uses either...or?
questions.explanation: Either is paired with or.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly uses neither...nor?
questions.explanation: Neither is paired with nor.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly uses not only...but also?
options: She is not only talented but also disciplined.
She is not only talented and also disciplined.
She is not only talented nor disciplined.
She is not only talented than disciplined.
questions.explanation: Not only...but also connects the two parallel adjectives.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly uses whether...or?
options: I wonder whether he stays and leaves.
I wonder whether he stays nor leaves.
I wonder whether he stays or leaves.
I wonder whether he stays than leaves.
questions.explanation: Whether is paired with or when presenting alternatives.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly uses would rather?
options: I would rather walking than driving.
I would rather walk than drive.
I would rather walked than drove.
I would rather to walk than drive.
questions.explanation: Would rather is followed by the base verb on both sides.

questions.questionText: Which sentence is correctly formed?
options: No sooner I had arrived than the meeting began.
No sooner had I arrived when the meeting began.
No sooner had I arrived than the meeting began.
No sooner did I arrived than the meeting began.
questions.explanation: Initial no sooner requires inversion and is paired with than.

questions.questionText: Which sentence is correctly formed?
options: Hardly had he finished when the bell rang.
Hardly he had finished when the bell rang.
Hardly had he finished than the bell rang.
Hardly did he finished when the bell rang.
questions.explanation: Hardly + had + subject + V3 is followed by when.

questions.questionText: Which sentence is correctly formed?
options: Scarcely she had left when he arrived.
Scarcely had she left when he arrived.
Scarcely had she left than he arrived.
Scarcely did she left when he arrived.
questions.explanation: Scarcely requires inversion and is paired with when.

questions.questionText: Which sentence best demonstrates parallel adjectives?
options: The examination was both difficult and interesting.
The examination was both difficult and interested.
The examination was both difficulty and interesting.
The examination was both difficult and to interest.
questions.explanation: Difficult and interesting are both adjectives.

questions.questionText: Which sentence contains a parallel verb structure?
questions.explanation: Studies and works are matching present-tense verb forms.

questions.questionText: Which sentence contains a noun-to-noun parallel structure?
options: Both the teacher and the student attended.
Both the teacher and studying attended.
Both teaching and the student attended.
Both teach and the student attended.
questions.explanation: The teacher and the student are both noun phrases.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly connects two verb phrases?
options: They will either travel by bus or travel by train.
They will either traveling by bus or travel by train.
They will either travel by bus or traveling by train.
They will either traveled by bus or travel by train.
questions.explanation: Both connected elements use parallel verb phrases.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly connects two clauses with either...or?
options: Either you study seriously or you will fail.
Either you study seriously nor you will fail.
Either you studying seriously or you will fail.
Either you study seriously and you will fail.
questions.explanation: Either...or can connect two complete clauses.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly uses not only at the beginning of a sentence?
options: Not only she passed, but she also won.
Not only did she pass, but she also won.
Not only she did pass, but she also won.
Not only passed she, but she also won.
questions.explanation: Initial not only in an emphatic clause commonly requires inversion.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly uses inversion after not only?
options: Not only is the book useful, but it is also affordable.
Not only the book is useful, but it is also affordable.
Not only useful is the book, but it is also affordable.
Not only does the book useful, but it is also affordable.
questions.explanation: The auxiliary is placed before the subject after initial not only.

questions.questionText: Which sentence does NOT require inversion because not only is in the normal middle position?
options: Not only did he study, but he also worked.
Not only was she tired, but she was also sick.
She is not only intelligent but also hardworking.
Not only has he arrived, but he has also called.
questions.explanation: Middle-position not only normally does not trigger inversion.

questions.questionText: Which sentence avoids an unnecessary double negative?
options: She doesn't speak neither French nor German.
She doesn't speak either French or German.
She speaks neither French nor German.
She doesn't speak neither French or German.
questions.explanation: Neither...nor already expresses negation.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly expresses two positive facts with emphasis?
options: He is not only punctual but also reliable.
He is neither punctual nor reliable.
He is either punctual or reliable.
He is whether punctual or reliable.
questions.explanation: Not only...but also emphasizes two true qualities.

questions.questionText: Which sentence expresses a choice between two alternatives?
options: Both the red and blue files are required.
Either the red file or the blue file is required.
Neither the red nor blue file is required.
Not only the red but also the blue file is required.
questions.explanation: Either...or presents alternatives.

questions.questionText: Which sentence means that neither of the two people attended?
options: Not only John but also Peter attended.
questions.explanation: Neither...nor means not one and not the other.

questions.questionText: Which sentence shows preference?
options: I would rather read than watch television.
I would rather read or watch television.
I would neither read nor watch television.
I would both read and watch television.
questions.explanation: Would rather...than expresses preference.

questions.questionText: Which sentence indicates that one event happened immediately after another?
options: No sooner had the plane landed than the passengers stood up.
No sooner had the plane landed when the passengers stood up.
No sooner the plane had landed than the passengers stood up.
No sooner did the plane landed than the passengers stood up.
questions.explanation: No sooner + had + subject + V3 + than describes immediate sequence.

questions.questionText: Which sentence indicates an almost immediate sequence using hardly?
options: Hardly had the match begun when it started raining.
Hardly had the match begun than it started raining.
Hardly the match had begun when it started raining.
Hardly did the match begun when it started raining.
questions.explanation: Hardly is followed by inversion and paired with when.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly expresses an almost immediate sequence using scarcely?
options: Scarcely had they entered when the lights went out.
Scarcely had they entered than the lights went out.
Scarcely they had entered when the lights went out.
Scarcely did they entered when the lights went out.
questions.explanation: Scarcely + inversion + when is the correct formal structure.

questions.questionText: Either the director or the assistants ___ expected to attend.
questions.explanation: The nearer subject, assistants, is plural.

questions.questionText: Either the assistants or the director ___ expected to attend.
questions.explanation: The nearer subject, director, is singular.

questions.questionText: Neither the players nor the coach ___ willing to accept the decision.
questions.explanation: The nearer subject, coach, is singular.

questions.questionText: Neither the coach nor the players ___ willing to accept the decision.
questions.explanation: The nearer subject, players, is plural.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly follows proximity agreement?
options: Either the engineers or the supervisor are responsible.
Either the engineers or the supervisor is responsible.
Either the engineer or the supervisors is responsible.
Neither the engineers nor the supervisor are responsible.
questions.explanation: The singular nearer subject supervisor takes is.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly follows proximity agreement?
options: Neither the supervisor nor the engineers is responsible.
Neither the supervisor nor the engineers are responsible.
Neither the supervisor or the engineers are responsible.
Neither the supervisors nor the engineer are responsible.
questions.explanation: The nearer subject engineers is plural, so are is used.

questions.questionText: Which option completes the sentence correctly? The researcher both ___ data and ___ the results.
questions.explanation: Both connected verbs should have the same grammatical form.

questions.questionText: Which option correctly completes the sentence? The students either ___ in the library or ___ at home.
questions.explanation: The two coordinated verbs must be parallel.

questions.questionText: Which sentence has the strongest parallel structure?
options: She wants both to study medicine and becoming a doctor.
She wants both studying medicine and to become a doctor.
She wants both to study medicine and to become a doctor.
She wants both study medicine and becoming a doctor.
questions.explanation: Both sides use matching to-infinitive phrases.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly uses parallel noun phrases?
options: The program benefits both students and teachers.
The program benefits both students and teaching.
The program benefits both studying and teachers.
The program benefits both student and to teach.
questions.explanation: Students and teachers are parallel noun phrases.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly uses parallel adjectives?
options: The task is both challenging and rewarding.
The task is both challenging and reward.
The task is both challenge and rewarding.
The task is both to challenge and rewarding.
questions.explanation: Challenging and rewarding are parallel adjectives.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly uses whether with infinitives?
options: She must decide whether studying or working.
She must decide whether to study or to work.
She must decide whether study or working.
She must decide whether to study nor to work.
questions.explanation: Whether can be followed by parallel to-infinitives.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly uses whether with clauses?
options: I do not know whether he will come or whether he will stay.
I do not know whether he will come nor he will stay.
I do not know whether he will come than he will stay.
I do not know whether he will come and whether he will stay.
questions.explanation: Whether...or connects alternative clauses.

questions.questionText: Which sentence expresses the meaning 'regardless of which alternative is true'?
options: Whether you agree or disagree, the decision will remain.
Either you agree and disagree, the decision will remain.
Neither you agree nor disagree, the decision will remain.
Both you agree or disagree, the decision will remain.
questions.explanation: Whether...or can express alternatives regardless of which is true.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly uses rather...than with parallel verbs?
options: He would rather resign than continue.
He would rather resign than continuing.
He would rather resigning than continue.
He would rather resigned than continuing.
questions.explanation: Would rather takes the base verb before than and after than.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly uses rather...than?
options: They would rather to wait than leave.
They would rather waiting than leaving.
They would rather wait than leave.
They would rather waited than left.
questions.explanation: The correct pattern is would rather + V1 + than + V1.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly uses no sooner?
options: No sooner had she finished the speech than the audience applauded.
No sooner had she finished the speech when the audience applauded.
No sooner she had finished the speech than the audience applauded.
No sooner did she finished the speech than the audience applauded.
questions.explanation: No sooner requires inversion and than.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly uses hardly?
options: Hardly had the examination begun when the fire alarm rang.
Hardly had the examination begun than the fire alarm rang.
Hardly the examination had begun when the fire alarm rang.
Hardly did the examination begun when the fire alarm rang.
questions.explanation: Hardly takes when and uses inversion when placed initially.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly uses scarcely?
options: Scarcely had the guests arrived when dinner was served.
Scarcely had the guests arrived than dinner was served.
Scarcely the guests had arrived when dinner was served.
Scarcely did the guests arrived when dinner was served.
questions.explanation: Scarcely takes when and requires inversion in this initial construction.

questions.questionText: Which fixed pair completes the sentence? ___ had the results been announced ___ the crowd began celebrating.
questions.explanation: No sooner is paired with than.

questions.questionText: Which fixed pair completes the sentence? ___ had he entered ___ the meeting began.
questions.explanation: Hardly is paired with when.

questions.questionText: Which fixed pair completes the sentence? ___ had the train departed ___ the passengers realized their mistake.
questions.explanation: Scarcely is paired with when.

questions.questionText: Which sentence contains an incorrect correlative pair?
options: Both the manager and the assistant agreed.
Either the manager or the assistant agreed.
Neither the manager or the assistant agreed.
Not only the manager but also the assistant agreed.
questions.explanation: Neither must be paired with nor, not or.

questions.questionText: Which sentence contains an incorrect correlative pair?
options: Both the old system and the new system work.
Either the old system or the new system works.
Neither the old system nor the new system works.
Both the old system or the new system works.
questions.explanation: Both must be paired with and.

questions.questionText: Which sentence contains an incorrect correlative pair?
options: She is not only smart but also patient.
She is either smart or patient.
She is neither smart nor patient.
She is not only smart and also patient.
questions.explanation: Not only is paired with but also.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly uses both...and with two clauses?
options: Both she passed the exam and she received a scholarship.
Both she passed the exam or she received a scholarship.
Both she passing the exam and received a scholarship.
Both she passes the exam nor she receives a scholarship.
questions.explanation: Both...and can connect two related positive clauses.

questions.questionText: Which sentence best maintains parallel structure?
options: The course teaches both writing essays and how to debate.
The course teaches both writing essays and debating.
The course teaches both write essays and debating.
The course teaches both writing essays and to debate.
questions.explanation: Writing and debating are matching gerund forms.

questions.questionText: Which sentence best maintains parallel structure?
options: The job requires not only patience but also working carefully.
The job requires not only patient but also careful.
The job requires not only patience but also carefulness.
The job requires not only to be patient but also working carefully.
questions.explanation: Patience and working carefully function as noun-like complements, though the structure is less perfectly balanced than simple noun pairs.

questions.questionText: Which sentence is most clearly parallel?
options: The athlete is both strong and endurance.
The athlete is both strong and enduring.
The athlete is both strength and enduring.
The athlete is both strongly and endurance.
questions.explanation: Strong and enduring are both adjective forms.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly connects two prepositional phrases?
options: The documents are stored both in the office and in the archive.
The documents are stored both in the office and the archive.
The documents are stored both the office and in the archive.
The documents are stored both in office or in archive.
questions.explanation: The two prepositional phrases are structurally parallel.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly connects two infinitive phrases?
options: He plans either to study abroad or to work locally.
He plans either studying abroad or to work locally.
He plans either to study abroad or working locally.
He plans either studied abroad or worked locally.
questions.explanation: Both alternatives use parallel to-infinitive phrases.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly connects two -ing phrases?
options: She enjoys both reading novels and watching films.
She enjoys both reading novels and to watch films.
She enjoys both to read novels and watching films.
She enjoys both read novels and watched films.
questions.explanation: Reading and watching are parallel gerund forms.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly uses neither...nor with verbs?
questions.explanation: Neither...nor connects the parallel verbs complained and left.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly uses not only...but also with verbs?
options: She not only sings but also dances.
She not only sings but also dancing.
She not only singing but also dances.
She not only sing but also dancing.
questions.explanation: Sings and dances are parallel verbs.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly uses either...or with verbs?
options: He either walks or takes the bus.
He either walks or taking the bus.
He either walking or takes the bus.
He either walked or taking the bus.
questions.explanation: Walks and takes are parallel present-tense verbs.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly uses both...and with verbs?
options: The researcher both collects and analyzes data.
The researcher both collects and analyzing data.
The researcher both collecting and analyzes data.
The researcher both collected and analyzing data.
questions.explanation: Collects and analyzes are parallel verbs.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly uses neither...nor with adjectives?
options: The explanation was neither clear nor convincing.
The explanation was neither clear or convincing.
The explanation was neither clearly nor convincing.
The explanation was neither clarity nor convincing.
questions.explanation: Clear and convincing are parallel adjectives.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly uses either...or with adjectives?
options: The answer is either correct or incorrect.
The answer is either correctly or incorrect.
The answer is either correct nor incorrect.
The answer is either correctness or incorrect.
questions.explanation: Correct and incorrect are parallel adjectives.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly uses not only...but also with noun phrases?
options: Not only the students but also the teachers attended.
Not only the students but also teaching attended.
Not only studying but also the teachers attended.
Not only the students or the teachers attended.
questions.explanation: The students and the teachers are parallel noun phrases.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly uses whether...or with two clauses?
options: Whether he comes or he stays, we will continue.
Whether he comes nor he stays, we will continue.
Whether he comes than he stays, we will continue.
Whether he coming or he stays, we will continue.
questions.explanation: Whether...or connects the two alternative clauses.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly uses whether...or with infinitives?
options: They must decide whether to stay or to leave.
They must decide whether staying or to leave.
They must decide whether to stay nor to leave.
They must decide whether stay or leaving.
questions.explanation: Whether can connect parallel to-infinitives.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly uses no sooner with inversion?
options: No sooner had the ceremony ended than everyone left.
No sooner the ceremony had ended than everyone left.
No sooner had the ceremony ended when everyone left.
No sooner did the ceremony ended than everyone left.
questions.explanation: Initial no sooner requires had before the subject and takes than.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly uses hardly with inversion?
options: Hardly had the teacher entered when the students became silent.
Hardly the teacher had entered when the students became silent.
Hardly had the teacher entered than the students became silent.
Hardly did the teacher entered when the students became silent.
questions.explanation: Hardly + had + subject + V3 + when is the correct structure.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly uses scarcely with inversion?
options: Scarcely had the film started when the power failed.
Scarcely the film had started when the power failed.
Scarcely had the film started than the power failed.
Scarcely did the film started when the power failed.
questions.explanation: Scarcely requires inversion and is paired with when.

questions.questionText: Which sentence is grammatically incorrect?
options: Both the father and the son were present.
Either the father or the son was present.
Neither the father nor the son was present.
Both the father or the son was present.
questions.explanation: Both must be paired with and.

questions.questionText: Which sentence is grammatically incorrect?
options: She likes both tea and coffee.
She likes either tea or coffee.
She likes neither tea nor coffee.
She likes neither tea or coffee.
questions.explanation: Neither must be followed by nor.

questions.questionText: Which sentence is grammatically incorrect?
options: I would rather stay than leave.
I would rather walk than drive.
I would rather staying than leaving.
I would rather study than watch television.
questions.explanation: Would rather requires base verbs, not -ing forms.

questions.questionText: Which sentence is grammatically incorrect?
options: No sooner had he arrived than she left.
Hardly had he arrived when she left.
Scarcely had he arrived when she left.
No sooner had he arrived when she left.
questions.explanation: No sooner is paired with than, not when.

questions.questionText: Which sentence is grammatically incorrect?
options: Hardly had I sat down when the phone rang.
Scarcely had I sat down when the phone rang.
No sooner had I sat down than the phone rang.
Hardly had I sat down than the phone rang.
questions.explanation: Hardly is paired with when.

questions.questionText: Which sentence is grammatically incorrect?
options: Both the plan and the budget were approved.
Either the plan or the budget was approved.
Neither the plan nor the budget was approved.
Both the plan and the budget was approved.
questions.explanation: Both...and takes a plural verb.

questions.questionText: Which sentence best demonstrates the difference between both...and and either...or?
options: Both means one alternative; either means both.
Both connects two positive elements; either presents alternatives.
Both expresses negation; either expresses preference.
Both requires nor; either requires and.
questions.explanation: Both...and combines two elements, while either...or presents alternatives.

questions.questionText: Which sentence best demonstrates the difference between neither...nor and either...or?
options: Neither...nor expresses two negative alternatives, while either...or presents alternatives.
Neither...nor expresses preference, while either...or expresses emphasis.
Neither...nor connects positive facts, while either...or connects negative facts.
Neither...nor and either...or always have identical meanings.
questions.explanation: Neither...nor excludes both alternatives; either...or presents alternatives.

questions.questionText: Which sentence best demonstrates the difference between not only...but also and both...and?
options: Not only...but also emphasizes the second element, while both...and simply joins two positive elements.
Both...and expresses alternatives, while not only...but also expresses negation.
Both...and requires inversion, while not only...but also never does.
They always have completely different grammatical structures.
questions.explanation: Not only...but also adds emphasis, especially to the second element.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly uses not only with inversion?
options: Not only did the candidate answer correctly, but she also explained the reasoning.
Not only the candidate did answer correctly, but she also explained the reasoning.
Not only did the candidate answered correctly, but she also explained the reasoning.
Not only answered did the candidate correctly, but she also explained the reasoning.
questions.explanation: Initial not only is followed by auxiliary + subject + base verb.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly uses not only with a linking verb?
options: Not only is the solution practical, but it is also inexpensive.
Not only the solution is practical, but it is also inexpensive.
Not only does the solution practical, but it is also inexpensive.
Not only is practical the solution, but it is also inexpensive.
questions.explanation: With be, inversion places is before the subject.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly preserves parallelism?
options: The manager wants employees to be punctual and working efficiently.
The manager wants employees to be punctual and to work efficiently.
The manager wants employees being punctual and to work efficiently.
The manager wants employees punctual and working efficiently.
questions.explanation: To be and to work are matching infinitive structures.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly preserves parallelism with adjectives?
options: The candidate was not only confident but also persuasive.
The candidate was not only confidently but also persuasive.
The candidate was not only confidence but also persuasive.
The candidate was not only confident but also persuasion.
questions.explanation: Confident and persuasive are both adjectives.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly preserves parallelism with nouns?
options: The committee discussed both the budget and the schedule.
The committee discussed both budgeting and the schedule.
The committee discussed both the budget and scheduling carefully.
The committee discussed both to budget and the schedule.
questions.explanation: The budget and the schedule are parallel noun phrases.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly preserves parallelism with clauses?
options: Either the company will expand or it will remain unchanged.
Either the company will expand or remaining unchanged.
Either the company expanding or it will remain unchanged.
Either the company will expand nor it will remain unchanged.
questions.explanation: Both alternatives are complete, parallel clauses.

questions.questionText: Which option best completes the sentence? ___ the evidence was incomplete, the conclusion was accepted.
questions.explanation: Whether can introduce an alternative clause, though the sentence requires a following or-clause for the full correlative construction.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly completes the correlative structure?
options: Whether the evidence is reliable or unreliable, the investigation must continue.
Whether the evidence is reliable nor unreliable, the investigation must continue.
Whether the evidence is reliable than unreliable, the investigation must continue.
Whether the evidence reliable or unreliable, the investigation must continue.
questions.explanation: Whether...or correctly presents the two alternatives.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly expresses preference between two actions?
options: She would rather revise the essay than submit it immediately.
She would rather revising the essay than submit it immediately.
She would rather revise the essay or submit it immediately.
She would rather revised the essay than submit it immediately.
questions.explanation: Would rather + base verb + than + base verb expresses preference.

title: Ethiopian English University Entrance Practice Test 6 2024
description: Ethiopian English University Entrance Practice Test 6 2024 featuring 100 authentic questions with step-by-step solutions. Designed for Ethiopian national exam mastery.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly compares the two laboratories?
options: Laboratory A is more modern than Laboratory B.
Laboratory A is most modern than Laboratory B.
Laboratory A is the more modernest than Laboratory B.
Laboratory A is as more modern as Laboratory B.
questions.explanation: Two things require the comparative form: more modern than.

questions.questionText: Of the four candidates, Hana is ___ at solving complex problems.
questions.explanation: A group of four requires the superlative: the most efficient.

questions.questionText: The second proposal is ___ practical than the first, although it is considerably more expensive.
questions.explanation: Two proposals require the comparative more practical.

questions.questionText: Which sentence uses the positive degree correctly?
options: The second machine is the fastest.
The second machine is more fast.
questions.explanation: Fast is the basic, non-comparative positive form.

questions.questionText: The blue route is ___ than the red route, but it takes longer because of traffic.
questions.explanation: A comparison between two routes requires shorter than.

questions.questionText: Among the five roads, this is ___ route to the airport.
questions.explanation: Among five roads, the superlative is required.

questions.questionText: Which form correctly completes the sequence: large → ___ → ___?
questions.explanation: Adjectives ending in -e take -r and -st.

questions.questionText: Which form correctly completes the sequence: happy → ___ → ___?
questions.explanation: With consonant + y, y changes to i before -er and -est.

questions.questionText: Which form correctly completes the sequence: thin → ___ → ___?
questions.explanation: The final consonant is doubled in the one-syllable CVC pattern.

questions.questionText: Which sentence is correctly formed?
options: This road is fastter than that one.
This road is more faster than that one.
This road is faster than that one.
This road is fastest than that one.
questions.explanation: Fast forms its comparative by adding -er without doubling the final consonant.

questions.questionText: The new building is ___ than the old one.
questions.explanation: Comfortable is a longer adjective and normally uses more.

questions.questionText: Of all the available computers, this model is ___.
questions.explanation: A group requires the superlative most expensive.

questions.questionText: Which sentence avoids a double comparison?
options: The revised method is more better.
The revised method is most better.
The revised method is more best.
questions.explanation: Better is already a comparative form.

questions.questionText: Which sentence is grammatically correct?
options: This is the most fastest vehicle.
This is the more fastest vehicle.
This is the most faster vehicle.
questions.explanation: Fastest already expresses the superlative, so another comparison marker is unnecessary.

questions.questionText: Which form is correct for the adjective careful?
questions.explanation: Careful normally uses more and most.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly compares the two narrow roads?
options: Road A is narrower than Road B.
Road A is narrowest than Road B.
Road A is more narrower than Road B.
Road A is most narrow than Road B.
questions.explanation: Narrow can take -er, giving narrower for two things.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly uses the irregular form of good?
options: This solution is gooder than that one.
This solution is better than that one.
This solution is more better than that one.
This solution is best than that one.
questions.explanation: The comparative of good is better.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly uses the superlative of bad?
options: It was the most bad result.
It was the worse result of all.
questions.explanation: The irregular superlative of bad is worst.

questions.questionText: The second examination was ___ than the first.
questions.explanation: The comparative of bad is worse.

questions.questionText: Of the three routes, the northern route is ___.
questions.explanation: Three routes require the superlative.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly completes the comparison?
options: Today I have less money than yesterday.
Today I have lesser money than yesterday.
Today I have least money than yesterday.
Today I have few money than yesterday.
questions.explanation: Less is the comparative form used with the uncountable noun money.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly uses the superlative form of little?
options: She has the most little money.
questions.explanation: The irregular superlative of little is least.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly uses the comparative of many?
options: She has manyer books than I do.
She has more books than I do.
She has most books than I do.
She has moreer books than I do.
questions.explanation: The comparative of many is more.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly uses the superlative of much?
questions.explanation: The superlative of much is most.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly uses a comparative with than?
options: The second exercise is difficult than the first.
The second exercise is more difficult than the first.
The second exercise is most difficult than the first.
The second exercise is more difficult as the first.
questions.explanation: A comparative is followed by than.

questions.questionText: Which sentence is the most formal complete comparison?
options: She is taller than I am.
She is tallest than I am.
She is as taller as I am.
questions.explanation: Than I am is the formal complete structure.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly uses a superlative?
options: He is tallest student in the class.
He is a tallest student in the class.
He is the tallest student in the class.
He is the taller student in the class.
questions.explanation: A superlative directly modifying a noun normally takes the.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly uses a possessive instead of the?
options: She is my the best friend.
She is best friend of mine.
questions.explanation: A possessive can replace the before a superlative.

questions.questionText: Which sentence expresses equal quality?
options: The two machines are as efficient as each other.
The two machines are more efficient as each other.
The two machines are efficienter than each other.
The two machines are most efficient as each other.
questions.explanation: Equality uses as + adjective + as.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly expresses inequality?
options: The red car is not as expensive as the blue car.
The red car is not as more expensive as the blue car.
The red car is not more expensive as the blue car.
The red car is not as expensive than the blue car.
questions.explanation: Negative equality uses not as + adjective + as.

questions.questionText: If A is not as fast as B, which statement must be true?
options: is not as fast as A.
questions.explanation: Not as fast as means the first item has a lower degree.

questions.questionText: If a book is not as interesting as another book, the second book is ___.
questions.explanation: If the first is not as interesting, the second is more interesting.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly intensifies a comparative?
options: The new system is much more reliable.
The new system is much most reliable.
The new system is more much reliable.
The new system is most more reliable.
questions.explanation: Much can intensify a comparative.

questions.questionText: Which sentence uses far correctly?
options: The new method is far more efficient.
The new method is far most efficient.
The new method is more far efficient.
The new method is far efficienter.
questions.explanation: Far can strongly modify a comparative.

questions.questionText: Which sentence expresses a small difference correctly?
options: The second option is slightly cheaper.
The second option is slightly cheapest.
The second option is more slightly cheap.
The second option is slightly most cheap.
questions.explanation: Slightly can modify a comparative to show a small difference.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly uses even with a comparative?
options: The situation became even more worse.
questions.explanation: Even can intensify a comparative; worse is already comparative.

questions.questionText: Which sentence shows a continuing change?
options: The weather is becoming cold and cold.
The weather is becoming colder and colder.
The weather is becoming more colder and colder.
The weather is becoming coldest and coldest.
questions.explanation: Short adjectives use comparative + and + comparative.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly expresses a continuing change with a long adjective?
options: The technology is becoming advanced and advanced.
The technology is becoming more and more advanced.
The technology is becoming more advanced and most advanced.
The technology is becoming advanceder and advanceder.
questions.explanation: Long adjectives use more and more + adjective.

questions.questionText: Choose the correct linked-comparison structure.
options: The more you study, the more you learn.
More you study, more you learn.
The most you study, the most you learn.
The more you study, more you learn.
questions.explanation: The structure is the + comparative clause, the + comparative clause.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly completes the relationship: 'The harder you work, ___'?
questions.explanation: Both clauses require the linked comparative structure.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly completes the relationship: 'The higher we go, ___'?
questions.explanation: Higher and colder are both comparative forms in the linked structure.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly uses a superlative with a defined set?
options: She is the tallest of the three sisters.
She is the tallest in the three sisters.
She is taller of the three sisters.
She is the most tall of three sisters.
questions.explanation: Of is used when selecting a member from a defined set.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly uses a superlative with a place?
options: This is the best restaurant of the city.
This is the best restaurant in the city.
This is the better restaurant in the city.
This is best restaurant of city.
questions.explanation: In is used with a place or context such as the city.

questions.questionText: Which sentence follows standard school grammar for comparing two alternatives?
options: Which is the biggest, A or B?
Which is bigger, A or B?
Which is most big, A or B?
Which is more biggest, A or B?
questions.explanation: School grammar normally uses the comparative for two things.

questions.questionText: Which sentence follows standard school grammar for three alternatives?
options: Which is bigger of the three?
Which is the biggest of the three?
Which is more bigger of the three?
Which is big of the three?
questions.explanation: Three or more normally require the superlative.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly compares quantities of countable nouns?
options: The second class has less students.
The second class has fewer students.
The second class has lesser students.
The second class has least students than the first.
questions.explanation: Students are countable plural, so fewer is used.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly compares quantities of an uncountable noun?
options: The second tank contains fewer water.
The second tank contains less water.
The second tank contains lesser water.
The second tank contains few water.
questions.explanation: Water is uncountable, so less is used.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly uses more with an uncountable noun?
options: We need more information before deciding.
We need more informations before deciding.
We need most information before deciding.
We need many information before deciding.
questions.explanation: More can be used with uncountable nouns such as information.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly uses more with a countable plural noun?
options: She bought more books than I did.
She bought more book than I did.
She bought most books than I did.
She bought more of book than I did.
questions.explanation: More can precede a plural countable noun.

questions.questionText: Which sentence uses most to mean a majority rather than a superlative?
options: She has the most books in the class.
He bought the most expensive book.
This is the most difficult question.
questions.explanation: Most students means the majority of students.

questions.questionText: Which sentence uses most as the greatest quantity within a group?
options: He has the most books in the class.
questions.explanation: The most books means the greatest quantity compared with others.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly uses as many?
options: I have as many books as my brother.
I have as much books as my brother.
I have as more books as my brother.
I have as most books as my brother.
questions.explanation: Books are plural countable nouns, so use as many.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly uses as much?
options: She has as many money as her sister.
She has as much money as her sister.
She has as more money as her sister.
She has as most money as her sister.
questions.explanation: Money is uncountable, so use as much.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly compares two amounts?
options: The company has fewer employees but less money.
The company has less employees but fewer money.
The company has fewer employees but fewer money.
The company has less employees but less money.
questions.explanation: Employees are countable; money is uncountable.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly uses a short adverb in the comparative?
options: She runs more fast than her sister.
She runs faster than her sister.
She runs fastest than her sister.
She runs fastly than her sister.
questions.explanation: Fast forms the comparative adverb faster.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly uses the comparative of hard as an adverb?
options: He works more hard than his brother.
He works harder than his brother.
He works hardest than his brother.
He works hardlier than his brother.
questions.explanation: Hard forms the comparative harder.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly compares the manner of two actions?
options: She completed the task more carefully than her colleague.
She completed the task carefuler than her colleague.
She completed the task most carefully than her colleague.
She completed the task more careful than her colleague.
questions.explanation: Carefully is a long adverb and uses more carefully.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly uses the superlative adverb?
options: She works the most efficiently in the team.
She works the efficientest in the team.
She works the more efficiently in the team.
She works most efficient in the team.
questions.explanation: Long adverbs use the most + adverb for the superlative.

questions.questionText: Which sentence contains the correct comparison?
options: He is taller as his brother.
He is taller than his brother.
He is as taller as his brother.
He is more taller than his brother.
questions.explanation: Comparatives are followed by than.

questions.questionText: Which sentence contains the correct equality structure?
options: She is as intelligent than her sister.
She is as more intelligent as her sister.
She is as intelligent as her sister.
She is more intelligent as her sister.
questions.explanation: Equality uses as + adjective + as.

questions.questionText: Which sentence contains a double comparison?
options: The new route is much shorter.
The new route is slightly shorter.
The new route is more easier.
The new route is far better.
questions.explanation: Easier already contains the comparative marker.

questions.questionText: Which sentence contains an incorrect superlative construction?
options: She is the best player on the team.
He is the most intelligent student.
This is the most easiest solution.
questions.explanation: Easiest is already superlative; most easiest is a double comparison.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly transforms 'John is taller than Peter'?
options: Peter is as tall as John.
Peter is the tallest than John.
questions.explanation: If John is taller, Peter is shorter.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly transforms 'John is taller than Peter' into a negative equality structure?
options: Peter is not as tall as John.
Peter is not as taller as John.
Peter is not taller as John.
Peter is not the tallest as John.
questions.explanation: The correct transformation is not as tall as.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly transforms 'This book is more expensive than that one'?
